WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The U.S. Navy has moved the guided-missile destroyer USS Cole and other ships to the eastern Mediterranean Sea off Lebanon, Pentagon officials said Thursday. "But it does signal that we're engaged and we are going to be in the vicinity, and that's a very important part of the world." The Cole was badly damaged by an al Qaeda bombing during a port call in Yemen in 2000, killing 17 sailors. It returned to service in 2002. The destroyer and two support ships are close to Lebanon but out of visual range of the coast, Pentagon officials said. Another six vessels, led by the amphibious assault ship USS Nassau, are close to Italy and steaming toward the other three, the officials said. And a Bush administration official told CNN the decision to move ships to the region was a message to neighboringSyria that "the U.S. is concerned about the situation in Lebanon, and we want to see the situation resolved." "We are sending a clear message for the need for stability," said the official, who was not authorized to speak for publication. The ships "should be there a while," the official added. Lebanon's pro-Western majority in parliament and the pro-Syrian opposition have battled for power over the last three years. The country has been without a president since November, when pro-Syrian leader Emile Lahoud's term expired and parliament was unable to agree on a replacement. Despite general agreement among the factions to award the post to army chief Gen. Michel Suleiman, disagreements over how to share power in a future Cabinet have kept the issue from coming up for a vote. Parliament speaker Nabih Berri's office announced Tuesday that the next planned session has been pushed back to March 11. Berri's office said the Arab League needed more time to break the deadlock. Lebanon has been wracked by a sometimes-violent power struggle since the 2005 assassination of former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, whose supporters blamed Damascus for his killing. WASHINGTON (CNN) — The U.S. Navy has moved the guided-missile destroyer USS Cole and other ships to the eastern Mediterranean Sea off the coast of Lebanon, Pentagon officials said Thursday.

A file image shows the USS Cole, which the Navy deployed to the Mediterranean off Lebanon.

The deployment comes amid a political standoff over Lebanon’s presidency, although the Navy would not say whether the events are linked.

“It’s a group of ships that will operate in the vicinity for a while, and as the ships in our Navy do, the presence is important,” Adm. Mike Mullen, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said Thursday.

“It isn’t meant to send any stronger signal than that,” he said. “But it does signal that we’re engaged and we are going to be in the vicinity, and that’s a very important part of the world.”

The Cole was badly damaged in an al Qaeda bombing during a port call in Yemen in 2000, which killed 17 sailors. It returned to service in 2002.

The destroyer and two support ships are near Lebanon but beyond visual range of the coast, Pentagon officials said. Another six vessels, led by the amphibious assault ship USS Nassau, are near Italy and steaming toward the other three ships, the officials added.

Mullen would not say whether the deployment was related to the upcoming Lebanese parliamentary vote on a new president, which was postponed for the 15th time earlier this week. He did, however, describe the vote as “important” and said Washington was waiting for it to take place.

A Bush administration official told CNN that the decision to move ships to the region was intended as a message to neighboring Syria that “the U.S. is concerned about the situation in Lebanon, and we want to see the situation resolved.”

“We are sending a clear message for the need for stability,” said the official, who was not authorized to speak for publication. The ships “should be there a while,” the official added.

Lebanon’s pro-Western parliamentary majority and its pro-Syrian opposition have battled for power over the past three years. The country has been without a president since November, when pro-Syrian leader Emile Lahoud’s term expired and parliament was unable to agree on a successor.

Although the factions have generally agreed to award the post to army chief Gen. Michel Suleiman, disagreements over how to share power in a future Cabinet have prevented the issue from coming to a vote.

The office of Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri announced Tuesday that the next planned session had been postponed until March 11. Berri’s office said the Arab League needed more time to break the deadlock.

Lebanon has been wracked by a sometimes-violent power struggle since the 2005 assassination of former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, whose supporters blamed Damascus for his killing. The resulting outcry eventually drove Syrian forces out of Lebanon, where they had been stationed since the 1970s.

outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — Pentagon officials said Thursday that the U.S. Navy had repositioned the guided-missile destroyer USS Cole, along with several other vessels, to the eastern Mediterranean near Lebanon.

The naval movement coincides with a political impasse over Lebanon’s presidency, although the Navy declined to say whether the two developments were connected.

Adm. Mike Mullen, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said the ships would remain in the area for some time and emphasized the significance of maintaining a U.S. naval presence.

He said the deployment was not intended to convey a message beyond demonstrating that the United States was involved, would remain nearby and considered the region highly important.

The USS Cole was severely damaged in 2000 when al Qaeda bombed it during a stop in a Yemeni port, killing 17 sailors. The destroyer returned to active duty in 2002.

According to Pentagon officials, the Cole and two support vessels were positioned near Lebanon but far enough offshore that they could not be seen from the coast. Six additional ships, headed by the amphibious assault vessel USS Nassau, were near Italy and traveling toward the other three.

Mullen would not comment on whether the deployment was related to Lebanon’s forthcoming parliamentary vote to select a new president. Earlier in the week, that vote was delayed for the 15th time. He did, however, describe the election as important and said Washington was waiting for it to occur.

A Bush administration official told CNN that sending the ships was intended to inform neighboring Syria that the United States was worried about events in Lebanon and wanted the crisis settled.

The official, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said Washington was delivering an unambiguous call for stability and added that the vessels were expected to stay in the region for a while.

For the previous three years, Lebanon’s pro-Western parliamentary majority and its pro-Syrian opposition had been locked in a contest for political control.

Lebanon had been without a president since November, when the term of pro-Syrian President Emile Lahoud ended and lawmakers failed to agree on a successor.

Although the rival sides broadly accepted army commander Gen. Michel Suleiman as the next president, disputes over the distribution of authority in a future Cabinet prevented parliament from holding a vote.

On Tuesday, the office of parliamentary speaker Nabih Berri announced that the next scheduled session had been postponed until March 11. His office said the Arab League required additional time to resolve the stalemate.

Lebanon’s political conflict, at times violent, had continued since former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri was assassinated in 2005. Hariri’s supporters accused Damascus of responsibility for his death.

Public anger following the killing ultimately forced Syrian troops to withdraw from Lebanon, where they had been deployed since the 1970s.

A file photograph showed the USS Cole, which the Navy had sent to Mediterranean waters near Lebanon.

CNN correspondent Zain Verjee contributed to the report.

outputs.L4:
The United States Navy deployed the guided-missile destroyer USS *Cole* and additional supporting vessels to the eastern Mediterranean as Lebanon’s political crisis continued without resolution. The ships were positioned in international waters near the Lebanese coast, although U.S. officials publicly characterized the deployment as part of routine naval operations and regional engagement rather than preparation for military action.

The move came as Lebanon remained without a president following the end of Emile Lahoud’s term in November 2007. Rival political blocs had agreed in principle that army commander General Michel Suleiman should become president, but repeated parliamentary sessions were postponed because the factions could not settle disputes over a new government, the division of cabinet seats, and electoral reforms. The impasse deepened tensions between the Western-backed government and the opposition, led in part by Hezbollah and supported by Syria and Iran.

Washington said the naval presence was intended to demonstrate its commitment to stability in Lebanon and the wider region. U.S. officials stressed that the ships would remain outside Lebanese territorial waters and that the deployment did not signal an imminent confrontation. Nevertheless, the arrival of the *Cole*—a destroyer previously targeted in a deadly 2000 bombing in Yemen—carried considerable symbolic weight.

The deployment was also widely viewed as a message to Damascus. The United States had long accused Syria of interfering in Lebanese politics and of supporting Hezbollah and other armed groups. By moving naval forces closer to Lebanon, Washington underscored its concern about outside pressure on the Lebanese government and its support for Lebanese sovereignty.

U.S. leaders called on Lebanon’s factions to reach a political settlement and elect a president without further delay. While presenting the naval movement as routine, the administration made clear that it was closely monitoring the standoff and wanted to discourage any escalation. The ships’ presence therefore combined reassurance for Washington’s allies with a warning to Syria and other regional actors that the United States remained engaged and expected Lebanon’s political crisis to be resolved peacefully.

## Why the US moved warships toward Lebanon during its presidential crisis

**BEIRUT —** The United States moved naval vessels toward Lebanon in early 2008 as the country’s parliament repeatedly postponed a vote to elect a president, deepening fears that the political stalemate could trigger renewed violence or invite greater outside interference.

The guided-missile destroyer **USS Cole**, accompanied by support ships, was sent into the eastern Mediterranean as part of what US officials described as a visible demonstration of Washington’s commitment to regional stability.

Lebanon had been without a president since **Emile Lahoud’s term ended in November 2007**. Parliament repeatedly delayed the election because rival political blocs could not agree on a power-sharing arrangement, even though army commander **Gen. Michel Suleiman** had emerged as a broadly accepted candidate.

The dispute pitted the Western- and Saudi-backed governing coalition against an opposition led by Hezbollah and supported by Syria and Iran. Washington accused Damascus of obstructing Lebanon’s political process and pressuring its government.

US officials said the naval deployment was intended to signal concern about the prolonged crisis and deter threats to Lebanon’s Western-backed government. Then-Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell said the ships were being positioned to demonstrate that the United States remained engaged in promoting stability in the region.

The move was not publicly presented as preparation for military intervention, and the ships remained in international waters. Still, their presence carried considerable symbolic weight in a country with a history of civil war, foreign military involvement and conflict with Israel.

Critics, including Hezbollah and Syrian officials, portrayed the deployment as intimidation and interference in Lebanon’s internal affairs. Supporters viewed it as a warning to regional powers not to exploit the presidential vacuum.

The crisis was ultimately resolved in **May 2008**, after deadly internal clashes and an Arab-mediated agreement in Doha. Parliament then elected Suleiman president, ending a six-month vacancy.
